transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Alex (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood Product), Riley (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Elena Morales (Pioneer CTO), Ibrahim Khan (Platform), Priya Desai (Data Scientist), Markus Lee (Security)

Summary:
Quick intro to Redwood's JSON-mode structured output and runtime fallback/guardrail patterns. Demonstration of typed responses, schema enforcement, and tool/function calling with fallbacks to simpler models. Addressed security/compliance concerns for regulated biotech workloads and discussed pilot next steps.

Topics covered:
- JSON mode and typed response schemas
- Tool/function calling flow and safety gates
- Fallbacks to quantized / cheaper variants under load
- Runtime observability in the Console + Optimize recommendations
- Security: KMS, audit logs, VPC/private deployment options

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, is this time still good?
[00:03] Elena (Pioneer): yeah this is fine, thank you jordan. we have a hard stop at 5:00 but should be okay.
[00:07] Jordan: perfect; quick round of intros — i am jordan patel, account exec, and alex is our solutions engineer who will demo the JSON mode and the fallback patterns. samir on product is here for deeper questions.
[00:18] Alex (SE): hi all, excited to walk through a couple patterns we've seen with biotech platform teams, especially around typed outputs and hooking functions for downstream pipelines.
[00:27] Ibrahim (Pioneer): great — from our side i'm ibrahim, i run the infra team. priya will be the main model consumer, markus handles security, and elena is overall owner.
[00:36] Alex: cool. so quick context check: are you evaluating hosted api or private deployment for pilot?
[00:41] Elena: initially hosted, but we will likely need private (vpc) for PHI-like metadata. we also want clear audit log and kms support.
[00:50] Jordan: understood — we'll show the hosted flow but call out parity for private and dedicated later.
[00:55] Priya: our key success criteria: deterministic JSON outputs for downstream parsers, ability to call our internal annotation tool, and predictable latency under batch loads. cost is also a factor.
[01:07] Alex: perfect. i'll start by showing a live schema demo in the Console — note: sometimes the transcript has odd names, sorry if a model name pops up weird.

[01:20] [screen share starts — Redwood Console shown]
[01:25] Alex: here is a prompt template with a json schema — we use typed contracts to force the model to return strictly-typed fields, for example sample_id, call_probability, recommended_action. you can choose enforcement modes: "soft" which scores and rewrites, or "strict" which invalidates and triggers fallback/runbook.
[01:40] Priya: if the model returns invalid json, does Redwood auto-correct or do we retry?
[01:44] Alex: there are a few paths — first we try a schema guided repair step locally, then if it still fails we can call a lightweight parser tool or route the request to a fallback model variant with higher decoding constraints. you can opt for automatic retry or surface the error to the app.
[01:58] Markus: can that fallback go to an on-prem quantized model?
[02:02] Alex: yes — the routing rules allow fallback to compatible model variants across hosted, dedicated pools, or private endpoints. we track runtime compatibility in the model catalog so a quantized on-prem replica that supports the same API can be targeted.
[02:15] Ibrahim: latency during retries is a concern — what are typical numbers?
[02:20] Alex: for strict enforcement we see tail latency increase for the individual request — a single repair+retry can add 150-300ms on average depending on sequence length. to mitigate we use prefix caching and continuous batching to keep token latency predictable.
[02:35] Samir (Product): and our Optimize product will give recommendations on batching and quantization to hit your cost/latency SLOs. we can simulate your token distribution during the pilot.

[02:48] [Demo: tool/function calling]
[02:51] Alex: next i'll demonstrate calling a function we registered — here the model returns the typed json and also indicates an action to call the annotation tool endpoint with params. the runtime validates the payload against the function spec before executing it.
[03:06] Priya: can we restrict which functions are callable per API key?
[03:10] Alex: yes — RBAC at the route and key level; you can white-list functions and services per tenant.
[03:15] Markus: what about data exfiltration prevention — e.g., model hallucinating a system command?
[03:20] Riley (Solutions): good question — we recommend a layered approach: 1) typed response schemas reduce free-text escape, 2) function spec validation ensures payloads match types, 3) runtime policies can block or sanitize requests to external functions and 4) an allow-list with audit logs. we also integrate with KMS for secrets so credentials never appear in plaintext.
[03:41] Ibrahim: can audit logs show the exact model output or just the validated payload?
[03:46] Riley: configurable — you can capture raw outputs for internal debugging, or redact and only store the validated/approved payloads for compliance. audit trails include timestamps, model id, and user key.

[04:00] [timestamp jump, demo continues]
[04:05] Alex: i'll intentionally force a malformed response to show repair and fallback.
[04:09] Alex (screen): sending request... model returned unclosed json, console triggers the repair pipeline, attempts a parse-only patch, still invalid, then routes to fallback model (smaller but stricter decoding). you can see the event in the trace — the call count increments and latency shows the retry.
[04:26] Elena: okay, that's useful. can we get alerts when fallback rates exceed threshold?
[04:30] Samir: yes — you can set alerts in Console for error rates, fallback percentage, and schema violation trends. Optimize will also recommend tuning prompts or model variants.
[04:42] Priya: from a data lineage perspective we want to tag where outputs came from — model version, quantization, A/B rollout groups.
[04:49] Alex: all captured, and you can link to traces for a request in Console.

[05:00] Markus: regarding encryption, do you support customer-managed keys for hosted?
[05:04] Jordan: we support KMS integrations and can use customer-managed keys for secrets and storage. for stronger controls we can propose a private deployment where keys stay in your VPC.

[05:15] Ibrahim: how about throughput? Our pipelines will submit bursts of 500 concurrent calls during peak experiments.
[05:22] Alex: Dedicated pools are best for predictable throughput. for hosted we can provision burst capacity — but for reproducible perf at 500 concurrent we recommend dedicated with configured autoscaling policies. We'll include capacity numbers in the pilot plan.

[05:36] [Discussion about pricing and pilot structure]
[05:38] Jordan: for the pilot we usually provide a 2-week sandbox tenant, recommended test harness, and we run a smoke benchmark. pricing depends on model selection and dedicated vs hosted. i'll follow up with an estimate.
[05:49] Priya: can we test both strict and soft enforcement to see downstream parsing error rates?
[05:54] Alex: absolutely — we can run A/B across enforcement modes and measure failure and recovery rates, also measure cost delta from retries.

[06:05] [Questions from Elena]
[06:07] Elena: who would be our main technical contact during pilot?
[06:09] Jordan: alex will be primary SE, riley for integration. samir can triage product-level questions.
[06:15] Elena: good. and how long would it take to spin up sandbox?
[06:18] Alex: normally 1-2 business days to provision a sandbox tenant with your sample schema and functions.

[06:25] [Minor cross-talk]
[06:30] Markus: also, do you keep data for debugging? retention windows?
[06:33] Riley: default retention for hosted logs is 30 days, but enterprise customers can request longer retention or log forwarding to their S3/partner. retention and redaction options are configurable.

[06:45] [Walkthrough of Console traces + Optimize suggestions]
[06:50] Samir: here's an Optimize recommendation — quantize this family of models to int8 for your workload and keep a small fp16 canary for safety. we'd expect a 2.5x throughput improvement on our benchmark for similar token lengths.
[07:05] Priya: what's the risk of quality drop with quantization for structured outputs?
[07:09] Alex: for typed jsons, we've seen when you tune prompts + strict schemas the quality drop is minimal; Optimize suggests a guardrail to run a small subset of requests through higher-fidelity model and compare.

[07:20] [Wrap-up / recap]
[07:22] Jordan: to recap — next steps are: we will provision a sandbox and sample project, run the A/B pilot for enforcement modes, share security docs, and provide pilot pricing.
[07:33] Elena: sounds good. Markus will send over compliance requirements and we will review the pilot plan internally.
[07:40] Jordan: excellent. we'll target the provisioning by end of week. thanks everyone.
[07:45] [meeting ends]
